claims.text: PtNi alloy nanoparticles with a Pt-rich surface will have greater HER activity than pure Pt nanoparticles.
PtNi alloy nanoparticles with a Pt-rich surface will have greater HOR activity than pure Pt nanoparticles.
PtNi alloy nanoparticles with a Pt-rich surface will be more durable than pure Pt nanoparticles during HER and HOR operation.
Thermal or chemical post-treatment induces Pt surface segregation and produces a Pt-rich shell over a Ni-rich core.
A Pt-rich surface over a Ni-rich core creates lattice strain.
A Ni-rich core beneath a Pt-rich surface creates electronic ligand effects at the catalyst surface.
The strain and ligand effects modify the hydrogen adsorption and desorption energy profile.
The Pt-skin provides hydrogen binding energies that lower the barriers for hydrogen adsorption and evolution.
Electronic and strain effects from the Ni-rich core stabilize the active Pt-rich surface.
Stabilization of the active surface reduces catalyst dissolution or deactivation during extended cycling.
Post-treated PtNi nanoparticles will exhibit lower HER and HOR overpotentials than pure Pt nanoparticles under identical acidic conditions.
Post-treated PtNi nanoparticles will exhibit improved Tafel slopes relative to pure Pt nanoparticles.
Post-treated PtNi nanoparticles will undergo less performance degradation during cycling than pure Pt nanoparticles.
The predicted advantages may not apply in alkaline electrolytes.
Incomplete formation of the Pt-skin may prevent the predicted advantages.

contradictions.description: The initial nanoparticles are described as a homogeneously mixed PtNi alloy while also being described as having Ni in the core and Pt distributed at the surface, which implies pre-existing compositional segregation rather than homogeneous mixing.
